title: Pilot Traffic Portrait & Success Metrics Sprint Planning — AmberLane Retail
summary: Kickoff to define success metrics and a sprint plan for a limited pilot that will characterize AmberLane's inference traffic. Primary objectives: collect representative request traces, agree on QPS/concurrency scenarios (peak/steady/burst), define token-length distributions for both inputs and responses, and schedule a 2-week benchmark sprint with a lab replay and Redwood-hosted comparison. Also agreed to exchange security docs for VPC/on-prem constraints.
next_steps: Redwood to share benchmark template and traffic-capture spec (Samir) — due 2026-02-02
AmberLane to export one week of anonymized request traces and sample prompts (Maya) — due 2026-02-05
Schedule 30m benchmark kickoff once traces received (Evan to schedule) — target 2026-02-09
Redwood to provide preliminary sizing estimate and cost model (Dana) — due 2026-02-06
Exchange SOC2/ISO audit snapshot and network diagram (Rita/Leo) — due 2026-02-04
action_items: Samir Patel: Send benchmark template + replay tooling notes — 2026-02-02
Maya Chen: Provide 7 days of anonymized inference logs + 50 sample prompts — 2026-02-05
Dana Ruiz: Draft initial GPU footprint and cost estimate for steady/peak/burst profiles — 2026-02-06
Evan Cho: Block calendar and set benchmark kickoff once traces land — 2026-02-09
Rita Gomez: Share security/architecture constraints (VPC, KMS, data residency) — 2026-02-04
transcript:
[00:00] Meeting header: 2026-01-28 08:00 PST | Duration: 46m | Attendees: Samir (Redwood AE), Dana (Redwood SE), Evan (Redwood Eng), Maya (AmberLane Head of ML), Leo (Platform Eng), Rita (CTO)
[00:12] Samir: hey everyone thanks for carving out time, um quick agenda — align on success criteria, traffic portrait, what we need for a 2-week sprint to benchmark, and security constraints. does that sound right to folks?
[00:26] Maya: yep that looks good, we're mostly here to figure out whether we can keep latency under 300ms p50 for chat flows and keep costs below our current per-req spending.
[00:38] Leo: and make sure whatever we do fits our VPC and KMS model, we can't tunnel traffic through a public shared plane.
[00:45] Dana: quick clarifying q: when you say chat flows, is that single-turn generate or multi-turn with context?
[00:50] Maya: mostly multi-turn, typical session length 3-6 turns, average input tokens maybe 40, response tokens 80, but variance is high for returns and product descriptions — some go to 400 tokens.
[01:07] Evan: okay good to note, any existing telemetry you can share — percentiles for qps or concurrency?
[01:12] Maya: currently very spiky during promotions — baseline qps ~8, peak bursts to 220 for short windows, concurrency we see 40-70 concurrent generation requests during peak, though long responses reduce throughput.
[01:28] Samir: perfect that's helpful, sounds like we should model three canonical profiles: steady (8 qps), peak sustained (40 qps for 10m?), and burst (220 qps for <2m). we'll also need token-length histograms.
[01:45] Rita: timeline constraint — we want a pilot running in prod lights for our holiday finals in mid-March, so ideally complete the benchmark + pilot sign-off by early March.
[01:55] Dana: that gives us six weeks, plausible. proposed plan: 1) collect traces and samples, 2) Redwood runs lab replay + config mapping, 3) joint benchmark (Redwood-hosted and on your dedicated if you want), 4) analyze results and define rollout.
[02:12] Leo: on the dedicated vs hosted question, we're leaning to private deployment in our VPC but want to compare delta in cost/latency vs Redwood hosted.
[02:23] Samir: totally, we often run that direct comparison. for VPC we need network diagrams and firewall rules, and we'll align on permitted egress for telemetry.
[02:34] Maya: one more security note — some prompts include PII (customer names, order numbers) so redaction in traces is needed.
[02:42] Samir: yes anonymization — send redaction rules, we'll accept a hashed id replacement.
[02:49] [03:00] Dana: technical question on model family — are you evaluating a single model or multiple variants for fallbacks?
[03:06] Maya: we want a primary open model plus a quantized smaller model as a fallback during extreme bursts if needed.
[03:13] Evan: that ties to throughput and kernels — smaller quantized models have different KV cache behavior and may not support long contexts as cleanly. we should capture context length distribution too.
[03:24] Leo: right now most sessions under 2k tokens context, but product search cases hit 4k+ occasionally.
[03:32] Samir: ok we'll model both 2k and 4k sequences in the replay.
[03:38] Maya: how do you handle batching — we expect low latency for interactive flows, batching can help cost but hurts p95.
[03:45] Dana: Redwood runtime supports continuous batching with latency SLO knobs; for interactive flows we recommend small max batch sizes and aggressive batching timeouts to balance cost. we'll show tradeoffs in the benchmark.
[03:58] [04:15] Evan: for sizing, I'm going to sketch three candidate footprints: "interactive" (low batch, higher GPU-per-qps), "balanced" (moderate batching), and "economy" (high batching or quantized small model). each will include concurrency curves and token throughput.
[04:35] Maya: curious about tail latency — our product is sensitive to p99 spikes. can we simulate real-world contention and long-running tokens?
[04:42] Samir: yes, part of the lab replay we'll inject tail requests — long responses, and token-heavy sequences to stress KV cache swapping.
[04:52] Leo: is there a recommended format for the traces? we currently have JSON lines with request_id, timestamp, prompt, response_len, user_id, session_id.
[04:59] Dana: that works, we'll provide a spec but JSONL with prompt (redacted), token counts, timestamps, and error flags is ideal.
[05:09] Maya: ok we'll strip PII and keep hashed ids.
[05:14] [06:00] Samir: success criteria — let's get explicit. Maya, what would make this pilot successful from AmberLane's perspective?
[06:08] Maya: top-level: 1) p50 < 300ms for interactive chat, p95 < 800ms; 2) cost per 1k tokens less than $X (we gave a target range in the doc but we'll confirm offline); 3) reliability 99.9% for the pilot traffic; 4) seamless network fit into our VPC with audit logs.
[06:25] Dana: we'll map those into test cutoffs for the benchmark; note that p95 target will be sensitive to token lengths and concurrency mix.
[06:34] Evan: for p99 we can run contention tests and a tail-latency heatmap to show how many qps we can sustain under X% of requests hitting >Y tokens.
[06:44] [07:20] Maya: timeline again — when do you need the telemetry by to hit early March?
[07:25] Samir: traces by 2026-02-05, bench kickoff 02-09, two-week sprint through 02-23, analysis and sizing by 02-27, sign-off early March.
[07:35] Rita: fine, but we need Redwood's cost model before committing.
[07:40] Dana: we'll provide an initial cost delta and note assumptions — model compute, batch config, quantization. we'll include sensitivity bands.
[07:49] [08:10] Leo: do you need real API keys or do replay from logs suffice?
[08:14] Evan: replay logs are fine; for VPC performance we may want to run a controlled test in your environment later.
[08:20] Samir: the replay tooling simulates client patterns and token timing so it's useful for initial sizing.
[08:26] [09:00] Dana: question on failure modes — do you have SLOs for model fallbacks or partial degrade?
[09:06] Maya: if primary model saturates, we can accept fallback to a smaller model with slightly lower quality, but we need to detect quality regressions automatically if fallback is used more than 5% of requests.
[09:19] Samir: Redwood Optimize can add monitoring hooks for quality drift tied to prompt sets. we'll include that as part of observability.
[09:27] [10:00] Evan: network note — for VPC we support private peering and a small agent; we do require an outbound port for telemetry if you want Redwood Console aggregation.
[10:12] Leo: we'll prefer S3-based log pickup and periodic pulls, less live telemetry during pilot to avoid audit approvals.
[10:19] Dana: that's fine, bench can run with S3 traces then.
[10:25] [12:00] Maya: let's talk about samples — we'll send 50 prompts that represent typical and edge-case flows. include examples that produce long token responses.
[12:09] Samir: great, also include failure/error cases and prompts with embedded JSON outputs you depend on.
[12:16] Maya: yes, some flows call downstream tools and expect structured outputs.
[12:21] Dana: we'll check function-calling compatibility in our replay; sometimes the tool calls magnify latency because of post-processing.
[12:31] [14:00] Evan: on benchmark metrics we'll produce: p50/p95/p99 latency, tokens/s sustained, GPU utilization, cost per 1k tokens, failed requests, and quality regression against a small eval set.
[14:14] Maya: for quality regression, what's the best approach? ROUGE or human eval?
[14:19] Dana: for structured outputs, automated syntactic checks and a small human spot-check sample (20 responses) are typical. we'll propose an eval rubric.
[14:30] [15:00] Samir: question for AmberLane: are there regulatory constraints for data residency?
[15:05] Rita: EU customers must stay in region; our primary market here is NA but we keep some EU data segmented. we'll mark that in the security doc.
[15:14] Samir: noted. we'll include region pinning in the sizing plan.
[15:22] [17:00] Leo: any requirements around audit logs retention?
[17:06] Rita: 12 months retention, immutable logs preferred.
[17:10] Dana: Redwood Console supports long-retention hooks as an add-on; we'll outline options and costs.
[17:18] [19:00] Maya: curious about quantization — if we use an int8 model as fallback how much throughput change do you typically see?
[19:06] Evan: int8 often gives 2-3x token throughput per GPU for sampling workloads but can increase variance in outputs, so we'll capture quality delta. depends on kernels and context size.
[19:24] Samir: we'll present a tradeoff matrix in the sizing doc.
[19:31] [21:00] Dana: for the replay tests, please label sessions that are interactive vs batch to help us set batching timeouts.
[21:07] Maya: will do.
[21:10] [23:00] Samir: quick note on costs — we'll produce a cost-per-1k-tokens baseline for hosted, and a dedicated private delta for reserved capacity with assumptions on committed concurrency.
[23:14] Leo: do you include network egress in your cost models?
[23:18] Samir: we'll present both compute-only and full-stack including egress, storage, and observability.
[23:26] [25:00] Rita: one last compliance Q: do you provide SOC2 report or ISO snapshot?
[25:06] Dana: yes we can share SOC2 Type II summary and an ISO attestation redacted copy. we'll add that to next steps.
[25:18] [27:00] Evan: operational playbook — we propose a staged rollout: bench -> small pilot (10% of traffic on canary) -> expanded pilot -> full prod. rollback policies and automated fallback to cheaper model are part of the plan.
[27:25] Maya: 10% canary sounds reasonable. what about the measurement window to judge canary?
[27:31] Dana: typically 24-72 hours with continuous quality checks and latency SLO monitoring.
[27:40] [30:00] Samir: ok let's recap action items and owners. Samir will send the benchmark template and replay instructions; Maya will provide traces and samples; Dana will draft the footprint and cost; Evan will schedule the bench kickoff; Rita/Leo will share security docs. deliverables dated in calendar invite.
[30:25] Maya: one logistical: we need non-disclosure language for traces — can you send an NDA excerpt?
[30:31] Samir: yes, we'll attach a short data-sharing addendum to the benchmark template.
[30:38] [33:00] Dana: small technical aside — when you anonymize, please keep token counts intact, don't truncate or compress prompts as that skews the replay.
[33:09] Leo: understood. we'll preserve tokenization boundaries.
[33:15] [36:00] Maya: ok final question: do you have any recommended thresholds for switching to fallback model during live traffic?
[36:06] Evan: operationally we recommend a forced fallback when sustained queue depth exceeds threshold for X seconds or when p99 crosses an absolute limit — we'll propose values in the playbook, but initial default: fallback if queue depth > 200ms of processing backlog for more than 10s. (note: this is heuristic, we'll tune.)
[36:30] Samir: and we can run chaos tests to validate graceful degradation.
[36:36] [40:00] Rita: thanks everyone, this was helpful. we'll get the traces redacted and send them early next week.
[40:07] Samir: thanks, we'll get the template over by Tuesday.
[40:12] Maya: great talk soon.
[40:15] [46:00] Meeting end — 46m total.
